questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: The Harappan civilisation is also known as the
questions.explanation: Its early sites were found in the Indus valley.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Harappa, the site that gave the civilisation its name, is located in present-day
questions.explanation: Harappa lies in the Punjab province of Pakistan.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Why did Harappan cities have drains covered with bricks or stone slabs?
options: To carry waste water away and keep streets clean
questions.explanation: Covered drains show attention to sanitation.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Which of these materials was used by Harappan craftsmen to make beads?
questions.explanation: Carnelian beads are well known from Harappan sites.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Mesopotamian records mention a distant land called Meluhha. Why is this of interest to historians of the Harappan civilisation?
options: It proves Meluhha was in Africa
It is often identified with the Indus region, so it suggests trade contact
questions.explanation: Meluhha is commonly linked with the Indus region.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Spindle whorls and remains of cotton have been found at Harappan sites. What can be inferred?
options: Cotton was grown and spun, so textile production existed
Cotton was imported only from Europe
questions.explanation: Cotton remains and spinning tools point to textile work.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: What were the citadel and the lower town in a Harappan city?
questions.answer: The citadel was a raised area to the west that held important public buildings. The lower town was a larger area to the east where most people lived and worked.
keyPoints: Citadel: raised area with public buildings
Lower town: residential and working area
questions.explanation: Many Harappan cities were divided in this way.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Why must historians be careful when saying that a Harappan object had a religious purpose?
questions.answer: The script cannot be read, so there are no texts to explain objects. Interpretations are often based on comparison with later practices and may not be correct, and an object may have had more than one use.
keyPoints: Comparison with later times may mislead
Objects may have had several uses
questions.explanation: Interpretation without written evidence is uncertain.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Mahavira is associated with which religion?
questions.explanation: Mahavira is regarded as the last Tirthankara of Jainism.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Where did the Buddha deliver his first sermon?
questions.explanation: The first sermon was at Sarnath, near Varanasi.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why is the Sanchi stupa important to historians?
options: Its sculptures show early Buddhist art and beliefs
It was built in the twentieth century
questions.explanation: The sculpted gateways depict scenes related to Buddhism.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Sangam literature belongs to which region of India?
questions.explanation: Sangam works were composed in Tamil.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why did Ashoka appoint officers called dhamma mahamattas?
options: To spread Dhamma and look after the welfare of people of different groups
questions.explanation: These officers helped carry out his policy of Dhamma.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why did Buddhism and Jainism gain followers among traders and ordinary people?
options: They were taught only in a language few knew
They used simple language, were open to many people and questioned rituals and birth-based distinctions
They were forced on people by the Harappans
questions.explanation: Accessible teachings appealed to a wide range of people.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Mention two sources historians use to study the Mauryan period.
questions.answer: Ashoka's inscriptions give direct evidence of his policies. Kautilya's Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indica as quoted by later writers, and archaeological remains are also used.
questions.explanation: Historians combine texts, inscriptions and remains.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Explain how coins, inscriptions and travellers' accounts together help historians reconstruct the past.
questions.answer: Coins show rulers, trade and the economy, inscriptions give official messages and grants, and travellers' accounts give an outsider's view. Comparing them helps check each source against the others and gives a fuller picture.
keyPoints: Travellers give outside views; compare sources
questions.explanation: Cross-checking sources makes conclusions more reliable.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded by
questions.explanation: The brothers Harihara and Bukka founded the empire in the fourteenth century.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Guru Nanak was the founder of
questions.explanation: Guru Nanak was the first Sikh Guru.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: With which of the following is Todar Mal associated under Akbar?
questions.explanation: Todar Mal was a revenue official who helped organise land revenue assessment.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Why did Akbar build the city of Fatehpur Sikri?
options: As a port on the Arabian Sea
As a fort on the Himalayas
As a capital near the dargah of Sheikh Salim Chishti
questions.explanation: Akbar built the city near the Sufi saint's dargah and made it his capital for some years.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Why did the Mughal state depend on zamindars?
options: They collected revenue and helped maintain local order, linking the state to the countryside
They had no role at all
questions.explanation: Zamindars were intermediaries between the state and the peasantry.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: How did Bhakti poets who composed in local languages help spread their ideas?
options: Only scholars of Sanskrit could follow them
People could understand the message directly without depending on Sanskrit
They were written in a lost script
questions.explanation: Local languages and songs made the message widely accessible.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Who was Mirabai and what is she known for?
questions.answer: Mirabai was a Bhakti poet-saint who composed devotional songs in praise of Krishna. Her bhajans are sung widely.
questions.explanation: Mirabai is a well-known figure of the Bhakti tradition.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Why is Ibn Battuta's account useful for studying the fourteenth century, and why should it be used with care?
questions.answer: Ibn Battuta, a traveller from Morocco, described the Delhi Sultanate's court, travel and daily life as an outsider. Since he wrote partly from memory and from his own viewpoint, his statements need to be checked against other sources.
keyPoints: Written from his own viewpoint and memory
questions.explanation: Every source has limits that must be weighed.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Which Governor-General introduced the system of Subsidiary Alliance?
questions.explanation: Wellesley used Subsidiary Alliances to extend Company control over Indian states.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: The Santhal rebellion of 1855-56 was a rising by
questions.explanation: The Santhals rose against exploitation by moneylenders and officials.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Which Governor-General is associated with the Doctrine of Lapse?
questions.explanation: Lord Dalhousie applied the doctrine to annex several states.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: The Deccan riots of 1875 were mainly directed against
questions.explanation: Peasants in parts of the Deccan attacked moneylenders to whom they were indebted.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: According to Macaulay's Minute of 1835, why was English education to be promoted?
options: To create a class of Indians who could assist in administration
questions.explanation: The aim was to train a class of intermediaries for the administration.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Which factor best explains why the 1857 revolt did not succeed?
options: It had a single unified command
It lacked unified leadership and coordination, and the British had greater resources and better communication
The rebels had more modern arms than the British
The British were absent from India
questions.explanation: Lack of coordination and weaker resources limited the rebels.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: State two causes of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: Political causes included annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse. Economic hardship for peasants and artisans, and resentment among sepoys, including the cartridge issue, also contributed.
questions.explanation: The revolt had several political, economic and military causes.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Describe two effects of the 1857 revolt on British policy in India.
questions.answer: Rule passed from the Company to the Crown in 1858. The army was reorganised with a larger share of British troops, and the government became more cautious about interfering in social and religious matters.
keyPoints: Transfer of rule to the Crown
Caution on social and religious matters
questions.explanation: The revolt reshaped the structure and policy of British rule.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
questions.explanation: The Congress was founded in 1885.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Which movement began after the partition of Bengal in 1905, with a boycott of foreign goods?
questions.explanation: Swadeshi promoted Indian goods and a boycott of British goods.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Who reorganised the Indian National Army in Southeast Asia during the Second World War?
questions.explanation: Subhas Chandra Bose took charge of the INA in 1943.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: From where did Gandhi begin the Dandi March on 12 March 1930?
questions.explanation: The march began at Sabarmati Ashram and ended at Dandi.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Why did Gandhi insist on non-violence even when it slowed the movement?
options: He had no interest in politics
He thought the British would leave in a day
He believed that means must be pure, and that violence would invite harsh repression and divide people
questions.explanation: For Gandhi, the methods mattered as much as the goals.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: What was a significant feature of the Government of India Act of 1935?
options: It provided for provincial autonomy, and elections were held in 1937
questions.explanation: Provincial governments were elected in 1937 under this Act.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Name any two leaders of the Moderate phase of the Congress.
questions.answer: Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale were Moderate leaders. Pherozeshah Mehta is another example.
keyPoints: Gopal Krishna Gokhale or Pherozeshah Mehta
questions.explanation: The Moderates led the early Congress.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Distinguish between the methods of the Moderates and the Extremists in the Congress.
questions.answer: The Moderates used petitions, prayers and constitutional methods to seek reforms. The Extremists, such as Tilak, favoured boycott, swadeshi and more active pressure, and aimed at swaraj.
questions.explanation: The two groups differed in approach and pace.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Who moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly in December 1946?
questions.explanation: Nehru moved the resolution that set the ideals for the Constitution.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: On which date did India become independent?
questions.explanation: India became independent on 15 August 1947.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Who was the last Viceroy of British India and the first Governor-General of independent India?
questions.explanation: Lord Mountbatten held both offices in 1947.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Through which amendment were Fundamental Duties added to the Constitution?
questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added the Fundamental Duties.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why did the framers include Directive Principles even though courts cannot enforce them?
options: They guide governments towards a welfare-oriented society and social justice
questions.explanation: They set goals for state policy.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why is the Preamble useful in understanding the Constitution?
options: It is a law that courts enforce above all others
It states the ideals and objectives that help in understanding the spirit of the provisions
questions.explanation: The Preamble summarises the values the Constitution aims to uphold.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: What are Fundamental Duties? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Fundamental Duties are obligations of citizens listed in Article 51A. Examples are respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, and protecting the environment.
keyPoints: Respect the Constitution, flag and anthem
questions.explanation: Duties complement the rights citizens enjoy.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: How did the framers try to accommodate India's diversity in the Constitution?
questions.answer: They adopted a federal structure with divided powers, guaranteed Fundamental Rights and cultural and educational rights for minorities, recognised several languages in the Eighth Schedule, and provided reservation for disadvantaged groups.
questions.explanation: The Constitution tries to balance unity with diversity.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: For how many years are members of the Lok Sabha elected?
questions.explanation: The normal term of the Lok Sabha is five years.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Who is the constitutional head of state in India?
questions.explanation: The President is the head of state.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Freedom of speech and expression falls under which group of Fundamental Rights?
questions.explanation: Article 19 lists the freedoms, including speech and expression.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Which Article prohibits the employment of children below fourteen years in factories and hazardous work?
questions.explanation: Article 24 forbids child labour in hazardous employment.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: President's rule in a state under Article 356 can be imposed when
options: the state has a new Chief Minister
the constitutional machinery in the state fails
questions.explanation: It applies when the state government cannot function according to the Constitution.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Why are seats reserved for women in panchayats?
options: To increase women's participation in local decision-making
To reduce the number of seats
questions.explanation: Reservation aims at greater representation and participation.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Name any four of the six Fundamental Rights.
questions.answer: The six Fundamental Rights are the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
keyPoints: Freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, constitutional remedies
questions.explanation: These six groups are in Part III.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: What is the anti-defection law and why was it introduced?
questions.answer: The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment in 1985, disqualifies a legislator who leaves the party on whose ticket he or she was elected, subject to conditions. It was meant to curb frequent switching of parties that made governments unstable.
questions.explanation: The law aims to protect the stability of governments.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Which body of the UN has representatives of all member states?
questions.explanation: All member states are represented in the General Assembly.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Along with Nehru and Tito, which leader was a founder of the Non-Aligned Movement?
questions.explanation: Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt was among the founders.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: What was the Marshall Plan of 1948?
options: United States economic aid to help rebuild Western European economies
A treaty between India and China
A plan to divide Germany permanently
questions.explanation: The plan gave US aid for post-war reconstruction.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: ASEAN is a regional organisation of countries in
questions.explanation: ASEAN groups the countries of Southeast Asia.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why did the Cold War not lead to a direct war between the USA and the USSR?
options: Nuclear weapons made a direct war too destructive for both
The UN forced them to disarm
questions.explanation: The danger of mutual destruction restrained direct conflict.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Non-alignment did not mean isolation for India because
options: India cut all contact with other countries
India engaged diplomatically and traded with both blocs while staying out of military alliances
questions.explanation: Non-alignment meant independence of policy, not withdrawal.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Name any three principal organs of the United Nations.
questions.answer: The General Assembly, the Security Council and the International Court of Justice are principal organs. The Economic and Social Council and the Secretariat are others.
keyPoints: International Court of Justice, ECOSOC or Secretariat
questions.explanation: The UN has six principal organs.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why do some countries ask for reform of the UN Security Council?
questions.answer: Its permanent membership reflects the world of 1945, and several regions and large countries have no permanent seat. The veto also lets one member block action, so reform is sought to make it more representative.
questions.explanation: The demand is for a more representative body.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Which type of settlement has houses scattered over fields, far from one another?
questions.explanation: Dispersed settlements have isolated houses or hamlets.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: The number of persons living per square kilometre is called
questions.explanation: That is the definition of population density.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Which of the following is a pull factor for migration?
questions.explanation: Better jobs attract migrants to a place.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Which set lists primary activities only?
questions.explanation: Primary activities draw directly on natural resources.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 40 and a death rate of 10 per thousand. Its natural growth rate per thousand is
questions.explanation: Growth rate = birth rate minus death rate = 30.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Why is population density very low in polar and desert regions?
options: Harsh climate and scarce food and water limit settlement
questions.explanation: Environmental limits restrict how many people can live there.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Differentiate between emigrants and immigrants.
questions.answer: Emigrants are people who leave a country or region to settle elsewhere. Immigrants are people who come to settle in a country or region.
questions.explanation: The terms depend on the point of view.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Explain two problems that rapid urbanisation can create in cities.
questions.answer: Rapid growth can cause a shortage of housing, leading to slums. It also strains water supply, transport and sanitation, and increases pollution.
keyPoints: Pressure on water, transport and sanitation
questions.explanation: Urban services often fail to keep up with growth.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
questions.explanation: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
questions.explanation: Coal is formed from ancient plant remains.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Jhum cultivation in north-eastern India is a form of
questions.explanation: Jhum is a type of shifting cultivation.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: The main raw materials of the iron and steel industry are
questions.explanation: Smelting iron ore needs coal for fuel and limestone as a flux.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Why does growing pulses in rotation with cereals help a farmer?
options: Pulses use up all the nitrogen
Pulses add nitrogen to the soil and help maintain fertility
questions.explanation: Pulse crops fix nitrogen in the soil.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Why are farmers who depend on rainfall alone vulnerable?
options: Rainfall can vary from year to year and harm crops
questions.explanation: Rain-fed farming is exposed to monsoon variation.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: State two differences between subsistence and commercial agriculture.
questions.answer: Subsistence farming is on small plots and mainly feeds the farmer's family, using simple tools and family labour. Commercial farming grows crops for sale in the market, using more capital, machinery and inputs.
keyPoints: Subsistence feeds the family; commercial sells
Simple tools versus machinery and capital
questions.explanation: The two differ in purpose and scale.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Why is the conservation of resources necessary? Suggest two measures.
questions.answer: Resources are limited and overuse can exhaust them or harm the environment, so future generations may be left without them. Measures include recycling, using renewable sources and avoiding waste.
questions.explanation: Conservation allows continued use over time.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Which railway crosses Russia from Moscow to the Pacific coast?
questions.explanation: The Trans-Siberian Railway links Moscow with Vladivostok.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: The Border Roads Organisation mainly builds roads in
questions.explanation: It builds roads in border and remote regions.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: National Waterway 1 runs along which river?
questions.explanation: National Waterway 1 runs along the Ganga from Haldia to Prayagraj.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Pipelines are mainly used to transport
options: liquids and gases such as oil and natural gas
questions.explanation: Pipelines carry fluids over long distances.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Why do landlocked countries depend on their neighbours for sea trade?
options: They have no coastline, so goods must pass through neighbouring ports
questions.explanation: Without a coast, access to the sea requires passage through other countries.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Two countries have the same per capita income but different life expectancy and literacy. What will the HDI show?
options: Different values, since HDI also counts health and education
questions.explanation: HDI combines income with health and education.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: State two advantages of water transport.
questions.answer: Water transport is cheap for carrying bulky goods over long distances. It also needs little energy per unit of cargo and does not need costly roads or rails.
questions.explanation: Ships and barges suit heavy cargo.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Why do countries form trade blocs? Give one example.
questions.answer: Member countries cut tariffs and barriers among themselves to enlarge their market and encourage trade and cooperation. The European Union and ASEAN are examples.
questions.explanation: Blocs aim to make trade easier among partners.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Which of these is a final good?
options: Bread bought by a household for its own use
Steel bought by a car factory
Cotton bought by a textile mill
questions.explanation: A final good is bought for consumption rather than further production.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Money that must be accepted in payment of debts by law is called
questions.explanation: Legal tender is money that the law requires to be accepted.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Which of these is a method of measuring GDP?
questions.explanation: GDP can be measured by the product, income or expenditure method.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Commercial banks earn profit mainly by
options: charging a higher rate of interest on loans than they pay on deposits
questions.explanation: The gap between lending and deposit rates is their main source of income.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.5 and investment rises by 100, the rise in income is
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2, so income rises by 200.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Why is GDP an imperfect measure of welfare?
options: It leaves out unpaid household work and says nothing on distribution or environmental harm
questions.explanation: GDP counts market output only and has important blind spots.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: State two functions of a central bank.
questions.answer: A central bank issues currency and acts as banker to the government. It also regulates commercial banks and controls credit and the money supply.
questions.explanation: The RBI performs these functions in India.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: How can double counting be avoided when measuring GDP? Give an example.
questions.answer: Only the value added at each stage is counted, or only final goods. If a farmer sells wheat worth 100, a miller flour worth 150 and a baker bread worth 200, the total value added is 100 + 50 + 50 = 200, the value of the bread.
keyPoints: Count only final goods or value added
Total equals value of final good
questions.explanation: Value added at all stages sums to the value of the final product.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Which of these is a capital receipt of the government?
questions.explanation: Borrowing creates a liability and is a capital receipt.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: In which year was the Planning Commission set up?
questions.explanation: The Planning Commission was set up in 1950.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Which of these is revenue expenditure?
options: Giving a loan to a state for a project
questions.explanation: Revenue expenditure is spending that does not create an asset, such as salaries.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: The balance of trade is a part of the
questions.explanation: Trade in goods is recorded in the current account.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: A government lowers import duties. What is a likely short-run effect?
options: Imports become cheaper and domestic producers face more competition
questions.explanation: Lower duties reduce import prices and increase competition.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Why did the government undertake disinvestment as part of reforms?
options: To increase taxes on the poor
To raise revenue and encourage efficiency through private participation in public enterprises
questions.explanation: Disinvestment means selling part of the government's stake in public enterprises.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Differentiate between revenue expenditure and capital expenditure.
questions.answer: Revenue expenditure is spending on day-to-day running of government, such as salaries and interest, and creates no asset. Capital expenditure is spending that creates assets or reduces liabilities, such as building roads.
keyPoints: Capital: creates assets or reduces liabilities
questions.explanation: The difference lies in whether an asset is created.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Why is a persistently high fiscal deficit considered a problem?
questions.answer: It means heavy borrowing, so interest payments grow and take a large part of future spending. It can also crowd out private investment and add to inflation.
questions.explanation: Large deficits can limit future government choices.
